binders: a ranges over arbitrary constant real-valued random variables; equivalently, an arbitrary real constant is viewed as a random variable [PDF page 19; printed page 30, phrase 'for any constant random variable a'].
C is an absolute constant independent of a in the expansion of the notation ≲ [PDF page 19; printed page 30, footnote 5].
hypotheses: The sole object-specific hypothesis is that a is a constant random variable; the passage imposes no centering, independence, or nonzero hypothesis [PDF page 19; printed page 30, sentence immediately after Equation (2.20)].
conclusions: The constant random variable a is sub-gaussian and its sub-gaussian norm obeys ‖a‖_{ψ2} ≲ |a|, i.e. there exists an absolute constant C such that ‖a‖_{ψ2} ≤ C|a| [PDF page 19; printed page 30, sentence immediately after Equation (2.20), together with footnote 5 and the cited Equation (2.17)].
The referenced bounded-variable estimate supplies the explicit admissible absolute constant C = 1/√(ln 2) for this upper bound [PDF page 16; printed page 27, Example 2.5.8(c), Equation (2.17)].
definitions_and_conventions: The sub-gaussian norm is ‖X‖_{ψ2} = inf {t > 0 : E exp(X²/t²) ≤ 2} [PDF page 16; printed page 27, Definition 2.5.6 and Equation (2.13)].
The comparison notation a ≲ b abbreviates a ≤ Cb for some absolute constant C [PDF page 19; printed page 30, footnote 5].
Equation (2.17) is the convention/result that a bounded random variable X is sub-gaussian with ‖X‖_{ψ2} ≤ (1/√(ln 2))‖X‖∞ [PDF page 16; printed page 27, Example 2.5.8(c)].
implicit_context: The underlying probability space and its measurability data are suppressed in the book's scalar random-variable notation [PDF page 19; printed page 30, phrase 'constant random variable a'].

The invocation of Equation (2.17) for a constant random variable uses the structural identity ‖a‖∞ = |a|; this identity is used by the source's immediate inference but is not separately displayed [PDF page 19; printed page 30, 'recall 2.17', and PDF page 16; printed page 27, Equation (2.17)].

Although the passage occurs inside the proof of the centering lemma and is next instantiated with a = E X, the stated constant-random-variable bound itself is quantified over every constant a and does not inherit the lemma's particular X as a hypothesis [PDF page 19; printed page 30, sentences following Equation (2.20)].

details: The phrase 'for any constant random variable a' is universal and includes a = 0; no exceptional constant is excluded [PDF page 19; printed page 30, sentence immediately after Equation (2.20)].
No fixed probability distribution, independence relation, or mean-zero condition is part of this subclaim [PDF page 19; printed page 30, the generic constant-random-variable sentence].
The symbol ≲ requires a multiplicative constant that is absolute, hence independent of a and of suppressed probability-space data [PDF page 19; printed page 30, footnote 5].
Equation (2.17) exhibits 1/√(ln 2) as a valid universal multiplier [PDF page 16; printed page 27, Example 2.5.8(c), Equation (2.17)].
The selected passage explicitly asserts an upper bound up to an absolute constant, not an equality or a lower bound [PDF page 19; printed page 30, ‖a‖_{ψ2} ≲ |a|].

The explicit value 1/√(ln 2) is justified as an admissible upper-bound constant by the cited bounded-variable result; the selected sentence does not claim optimality or exact norm evaluation [PDF page 16; printed page 27, Equation (2.17), and PDF page 19; printed page 30, the ≲ statement].

The letter a denotes the value of a constant random variable, so |a| is a scalar absolute value while ‖a‖_{ψ2} is the random variable's sub-gaussian norm [PDF page 19; printed page 30, constant-random-variable sentence].

undebatable_constraints: The claim must range over every constant random variable a, including zero [PDF page 19; printed page 30, 'for any constant random variable a'].

The required relation is the upper bound ‖a‖_{ψ2} ≤ C|a| for an absolute constant C; neither equality nor a reverse inequality is asserted [PDF page 19; printed page 30, constant-random-variable sentence and footnote 5].
The constant cannot depend on a; the source explicitly calls it absolute [PDF page 19; printed page 30, footnote 5].
An admissible explicit choice is C = 1/√(ln 2), obtained from the cited bounded-variable inequality (2.17) [PDF page 16; printed page 27, Example 2.5.8(c), Equation (2.17)].
No centering, independence, mean-zero, or nonzero assumption may be added to this generic constant-random-variable subclaim [PDF page 19; printed page 30, sentence immediately after Equation (2.20)].
The ψ2 norm is governed by the exponential-moment definition ‖X‖_{ψ2} = inf {t > 0 : E exp(X²/t²) ≤ 2} [PDF page 16; printed page 27, Definition 2.5.6 and Equation (2.13)].

ambiguities.issue: The prepared locator labels Equation (2.17) as the definition of the ψ2 norm, but the authoritative page places that definition at Equation (2.13); Equation (2.17) is instead the bounded-random-variable estimate.
ambiguities.evidence: PDF page 16; printed page 27: Definition 2.5.6 displays the norm definition as (2.13), while Example 2.5.8(c) labels ‖X‖_{ψ2} ≤ C‖X‖∞ as (2.17).
ambiguities.impact: Use Equation (2.13) to interpret the norm and Equation (2.17) to justify the constant-variable upper bound; treating (2.17) itself as the definition would misidentify the source structure.

ambiguities.issue: The selected sentence uses the coarse comparison ≲ even though its cited Equation (2.17) exhibits a particular valid constant.
ambiguities.evidence: PDF page 19; printed page 30 states ‖a‖_{ψ2} ≲ |a| and footnote 5 expands ≲ existentially; PDF page 16; printed page 27 gives C = 1/√(ln 2) in Equation (2.17).
ambiguities.impact: The source contract requires existence of an absolute upper-bound constant and recognizes 1/√(ln 2) as an explicit admissible witness, but it must not upgrade the selected claim to exact equality or optimality.

contract_plain_english: For every real constant viewed as a random variable, its ψ2 norm is at most an absolute constant times its absolute value. The referenced bounded-variable estimate gives 1/√(ln 2) as a valid universal multiplier. The statement has no centering, independence, mean-zero, or nonzero assumption, and it asserts only an upper bound, not equality.
